title: MQTT Protocol
subtitle: Publish-subscribe messaging for IoT — broker, QoS, topics, and Home Assistant integration
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: IoT systems have many sensors and actuators that need to communicate with each other and with dashboards/automation systems. HTTP polling is too heavy for constrained devices. Direct device-to-device is too complex to coordinate. You need a lightweight message bus.
whyItExists.solution: MQTT is a publish-subscribe protocol designed specifically for IoT. Devices publish messages to topics; any interested subscriber receives them. A central broker (Mosquitto) routes everything. It uses <1 KB RAM and handles unreliable networks gracefully.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any IoT system with multiple sensors and actuators, home automation (Home Assistant), industrial telemetry, fleet management, or any device-to-cloud communication.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Synchronous request-response (use HTTP/REST). Real-time bi-directional streaming (use WebSocket). Devices without IP networking (use RS-485, CAN, Zigbee).

explainModes.beginner: MQTT works like a radio station. Sensors (publishers) broadcast on channels (topics) like 'home/living-room/temperature'. Dashboards (subscribers) tune in to those channels and receive every broadcast. The broker is like the radio tower that routes signals between everyone.
explainModes.simple: Every MQTT device connects to a central broker (server). Publishers send messages to named topics (e.g., 'sensors/01/temp'). Subscribers register interest in topics using wildcards (sensors/#). The broker delivers every published message to all matching subscribers.
explainModes.standard: MQTT uses a client-server model where the server (broker) is the hub. All clients connect to the broker via TCP port 1883 (or 8883 for TLS). Messages have: topic (hierarchical string path), payload (up to 256 MB, usually JSON), QoS level (0/1/2), and optional retain flag.
explainModes.technical: MQTT CONNECT packet carries clientId, username, password, keepalive. QoS 0 = fire-and-forget (no ACK). QoS 1 = at-least-once (PUBACK, may duplicate). QoS 2 = exactly-once (four-way PUBREC/PUBREL/PUBCOMP handshake). Retained messages are stored by broker and delivered to new subscribers immediately on subscribe. Last Will and Testament (LWT) lets devices publish a 'gone offline' message on unexpected disconnect.
explainModes.deepDive: MQTT 5.0 adds: message expiry interval, topic aliases (reduce packet size), user properties (key-value metadata), shared subscriptions (load balancing across subscribers), flow control, and reason codes for diagnostics. For large deployments, EMQX or VerneMQ support horizontal clustering to millions of connections. MQTT over WebSocket (port 443) allows browser clients (mqttws31.min.js, MQTT.js) without special firewall rules.

content.text: How MQTT Works: Broker, Topics, Pub/Sub

MQTT is a publish-subscribe protocol. Publishers send messages to topics (hierarchical paths like home/kitchen/temperature). Subscribers receive messages from topics they've registered interest in. The broker (server) routes all messages between clients. No publisher needs to know who subscribes — full decoupling.

content.code:
MQTT Topic Structure
────────────────────
home/living-room/temperature   → specific sensor
home/living-room/humidity
home/kitchen/temperature
home/#                         → all home/ subtopics (# wildcard)
home/+/temperature             → temperature from any room (+ single-level wildcard)

Common IoT topic conventions:
cmnd/device-id/POWER           → Tasmota: command to turn on
stat/device-id/RESULT          → Tasmota: status result
homeassistant/sensor/01/state  → Home Assistant auto-discovery

content.text: Installing Mosquitto Broker on Raspberry Pi

content.code:
# Install Mosquitto MQTT broker
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y mosquitto mosquitto-clients

# Start and enable at boot
sudo systemctl enable --now mosquitto

# Configure: allow anonymous connections on localhost
# (add auth for internet-facing brokers)
echo "allow_anonymous true" | sudo tee /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/local.conf
echo "listener 1883" >> /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/local.conf
sudo systemctl restart mosquitto

# Test: open two terminals
# Terminal 1 — subscribe:
mosquitto_sub -h localhost -t "test/#" -v

# Terminal 2 — publish:
mosquitto_pub -h localhost -t "test/hello" -m '{"value": 42}'
# Terminal 1 should receive: test/hello {"value": 42}

content.text: Python MQTT Publisher: Sending Sensor Data

content.code:
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json
import time
import random

# Install: pip install paho-mqtt
BROKER   = "localhost"  # or your Pi's IP from other devices
PORT     = 1883
CLIENT_ID = "sensor-01"

client = mqtt.Client(mqtt.CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2, CLIENT_ID)

# Optional: last will message (sent if client disconnects unexpectedly)
client.will_set(
    f"home/sensors/{CLIENT_ID}/status",
    payload=json.dumps({"online": False}),
    qos=1, retain=True
)

client.connect(BROKER, PORT, keepalive=60)
client.loop_start()  # start background thread for MQTT

# Publish online status
client.publish(
    f"home/sensors/{CLIENT_ID}/status",
    json.dumps({"online": True}),
    qos=1, retain=True
)

try:
    while True:
        payload = json.dumps({
            "temperature": round(20 + random.uniform(0, 10), 1),
            "humidity":    round(40 + random.uniform(0, 30), 1),
            "uptime":      int(time.time())
        })
        result = client.publish(f"home/sensors/{CLIENT_ID}/data", payload, qos=1)
        print(f"Published: {payload} [rc={result.rc}]")
        time.sleep(5)

except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print("Stopping...")
finally:
    client.loop_stop()
    client.disconnect()

content.text: Python MQTT Subscriber: Receiving and Acting on Data

content.code:
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json

BROKER = "localhost"

def on_connect(client, userdata, flags, reason_code, properties):
    print(f"Connected: {reason_code}")
    # Subscribe in on_connect so it re-subscribes after reconnect
    client.subscribe("home/#", qos=1)
    print("Subscribed to home/#")

def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    topic   = msg.topic
    payload = msg.payload.decode("utf-8")

    try:
        data = json.loads(payload)
        if "temperature" in data:
            temp = data["temperature"]
            print(f"[{topic}] Temperature: {temp}°C", end="")
            if temp > 28:
                print(" ⚠ HIGH TEMP — triggering cooling fan")
                client.publish("home/actuators/fan", json.dumps({"on": True}), qos=1)
            else:
                print()
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print(f"[{topic}] Raw: {payload}")

client = mqtt.Client(mqtt.CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2, "dashboard-01")
client.on_connect = on_connect
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect(BROKER, 1883, keepalive=60)
client.loop_forever()  # blocking

content.title: MQTT QoS 0 vs QoS 1 vs QoS 2

a.name: QoS 0 — At Most Once
strengths: Best for high-frequency data (10+ per second)
weaknesses: Message may be lost if connection drops
a.useWhen: Live telemetry where a missed reading is acceptable (temperature updates)

b.name: QoS 1 — At Least Once
weaknesses: May deliver duplicates — receiver must be idempotent
b.useWhen: Sensor data you must not lose: alarms, door events, billing meters

content.text: Use `retain=True` on status topics (online/offline, current setpoint) so new subscribers immediately get the last value without waiting for the next publish. Retained messages are stored by the broker and delivered instantly on subscribe.

questions.question: What is an MQTT broker?
options: The central server that receives messages and routes them to matching subscribers
A protocol for I2C bus communication
questions.explanation: The MQTT broker is the message hub. Publishers send to it; it delivers to all matching subscribers. Mosquitto and EMQX are popular open-source brokers.

questions.question: What does the topic wildcard 'home/+/temperature' match?
options: Any single-level subtopic of home/ followed by /temperature (e.g. home/kitchen/temperature)
All temperature topics regardless of prefix
questions.explanation: The + wildcard matches exactly one level. home/+/temperature matches home/kitchen/temperature, home/living-room/temperature, etc., but NOT home/floor1/room2/temperature (that would need home/#).

questions.question: What is a 'retained message' in MQTT?
options: A message held in a queue due to network failure
A message stored by the broker and immediately sent to any new subscriber to that topic
A message with QoS 2 delivery guarantee
questions.explanation: A retained message (publish with retain=True) is stored by the broker as the 'last known value'. When a new client subscribes to that topic, it receives the retained message immediately — without waiting for the next publish.

faq.a: Quality of Service: QoS 0 = at most once (no guarantee, fastest), QoS 1 = at least once (may duplicate, guaranteed delivery), QoS 2 = exactly once (slowest, four-way handshake). Use QoS 1 for most IoT data; QoS 2 only for billing or financial messages.

faq.q: How do I secure my MQTT broker so only my devices can connect?
faq.a: Add password authentication to Mosquitto: create a password file with `mosquitto_passwd -c /etc/mosquitto/passwd myuser`, add `password_file /etc/mosquitto/passwd` and `allow_anonymous false` to mosquitto.conf. For internet-facing brokers, also enable TLS on port 8883 using Let's Encrypt certificates.

faq.q: Can I use a cloud MQTT broker instead of running Mosquitto locally?
faq.a: Yes. HiveMQ Cloud (free tier), EMQX Cloud, and AWS IoT Core offer hosted MQTT brokers. Use them when devices are outside your local network. The paho-mqtt client code is the same — just change the broker hostname, port, and add TLS/authentication.
